items.title: Can AI generate good designs from raw user data
summary: NN/g gave an AI two design tasks, a rebooking form and a checkout flow.
Designs were better when the AI got synthesized findings and recommendations.
Raw user comments alone produced weaker interfaces, so synthesis still matters.

why.ai-prototyping: It shows that feeding AI prototype tools synthesized research gives better output than dumping raw feedback on them.
why.research: It makes a concrete case that research synthesis remains valuable even when AI can read raw data.
why.general: Good inputs still decide good AI-generated design, so keep doing the synthesis step.

items.title: Qualitative user research methods overview
summary: Covers usability testing, user interviews, field studies and diary studies.
Estimates the rough relative cost and difficulty of each method.
Companion piece to NN/g's overview of quantitative methods.

why.research: A quick reference for picking the right qualitative method when you need to learn why users struggle.
why.general: Useful for choosing a method before you plan your next study.

items.title: Design by playground
summary: Designers now use AI coding agents to build small, disposable design tools.
Playgrounds let you tweak variables and states with real content and data.
Building one used to cost too much time, and now takes minutes.

why.ai-prototyping: It describes a practical way to explore edge cases, animation and states that static mockups hide.
why.craft: Real data and adjustable controls surface long names, empty states and errors before developers flag them.
why.general: A new habit worth trying for a single tricky design question.

items.title: Prototypes are the best specification, especially with AI
summary: When building takes an afternoon, a working version can come before requirements.
Open questions in a spec often answer themselves once you can click it.
Designers, PMs and engineers can all build prototypes now, so teams must adapt.

why.ai-prototyping: It argues the spec now records what building settled instead of predicting it.
why.product-strategy: It challenges the write requirements, sign off, then build sequence many teams still follow.
why.general: Expect more working prototypes to show up before documents do.

items.title: The attack of the giant AI design slop monster
summary: Author expands a conference talk on how AI changed UX design in 2026.
In research, hallucinated quotes are gone and reports are easy with templates.
Human oversight and interpretation still matter, while AI design is no longer dismissable.

why.ai-interaction: A practitioner's candid view of how fast AI for design moved in one year.
why.craft: It raises the quality question when AI-made design floods products.
why.general: Useful perspective on where professional judgement still counts.

items.title: Meta's Muse launch with Mona Sarantakos
summary: Muse is the number one App Store app and a fast-growing AI consumer product.
The team waited seven months to launch and uses agent swarms for insights.
The episode covers two levers that move activation for an AI agent.

why.growth: It looks at what moves activation for an AI agent product at big consumer scale.
why.ai-interaction: It shows how a team shaped an agent product, from avatar to unexpected use cases.
why.general: A rare inside look at a major AI consumer launch.

items.title: What it takes to be a great PM in the AI era
summary: Atlassian's head of AI and product craft says a PM's first job is a shared brain.
He describes three PM types, the artist, the scientist and the GM.
Atlassian is hiring more juniors than ever and PM roles are growing fast.

why.product-strategy: It offers a view on how PM work and hiring are changing as AI products spread.
why.leadership: It covers common mistakes new PM managers make.
why.general: Helpful for anyone working closely with PMs.

items.title: Users rubber stamp AI permission requests
summary: Users tend to approve AI permission requests without really reading them.
Nielsen suggests asking for permissions in context, one at a time.
The roundup also covers speed as good UX and using AI to prepare for conversations.

why.trust: A barrage of permission prompts trains people to click yes, which weakens real consent.
why.ai-interaction: It points to a concrete pattern for agent permission design, asking at the moment of need.
why.general: Worth checking how your agent asks for access.

items.title: Service as software and outcome pricing
summary: AI vendors now sell finished work and charge per outcome.
Outcome pricing moves the cost of failed work onto the seller.
Uncounted phantom resolutions stay the buyer's problem, so designing the meter is UX work.

why.product-strategy: Pricing per outcome changes what teams must measure and show to customers.
why.trust: Phantom resolutions can erode confidence unless the meter is clear and auditable.
why.general: Designing and auditing the meter becomes part of the job.

items.title: Crazy Agent Scale lessons from companies all in on AI
summary: Notes from an event on pushing AI agents to their limits.
Keep specs outside the context window so agents can read and edit them.
Adversarial pairs, like a PM who only critiques, improve agent output.

why.ai-interaction: Concrete patterns for orchestrating many agents that designers of agent products can borrow.
why.general: A look at how heavy agent users actually work.

items.title: How I fight token fraud as a solo founder
summary: The ChatPRD founder describes six abuse patterns that cost tens of thousands of dollars.
Fraudsters farmed free trials, resold promo codes and ran a custom MCP.
She ended free trials for good, since if you sell AI, you sell compute.

why.product-strategy: Free trials and support desks in AI products carry real compute cost and abuse risk.
why.growth: It challenges the usual free trial growth tactic for AI products.
why.general: Worth knowing before you plan AI onboarding.

items.title: Send the firefighters to the fires
summary: If a user's job is fixing what's broken, show what's broken first.
Enterprise software often sorts for the data model, buyer demo or shipping team.
Start from the user's job, using Jobs to Be Done thinking.

why.craft: A clear principle for triage screens like compliance, invoices and tickets.
why.product-strategy: It ties interface priority to the job users are actually hired to do.
why.general: A good check for any list-heavy enterprise view.

items.title: What is a researcher's worth
summary: Debate over research value is about more than AI replacing jobs.
Researchers face doubts about methods, representativeness and truthfulness of participants.
The author argues effortless AI makes human friction our scarcest asset.

why.research: It frames how to argue for research value as AI makes insight cheap to produce.
why.leadership: Helps leads think about research maturity and how to defend the practice.
why.general: A reflective read on the researcher's role.

items.title: AI sped up the build, so can accessibility testing keep up
summary: A survey of 2,500 professionals found AI sped up design, planning and development.
Only 30 percent said AI sped up QA and testing.
WebAIM found detected errors per home page rose from 51 to 56.1.

why.accessibility: Faster builds without faster checks mean accessibility problems may pile up late.
why.ai-quality: It shows validation lags behind generation in AI-assisted workflows.
why.general: Think about where accessibility checks sit now. This is a sponsored article.

items.title: Sabre wants to power AI travel bookings
summary: AI platforms could become a new front door for travel bookings.
Sabre wants to handle the transactions behind those bookings.
Someone else may control the customer relationship.

why.ai-travel-commerce: It shows who may own booking infrastructure and customer relationships if AI assistants become the entry point.
why.general: Relevant to anyone designing commerce flows that agents may sit in front of.

items.title: Airbnb floats price matching as AI agents loom
summary: Airbnb is floating the idea of price matching.
Skift ran a test of where direct booking wins.
AI agents may force a best price guarantee for short-term rentals.

why.ai-travel-commerce: Agents that compare prices put pressure on platforms to guarantee the best rate.
why.general: A sign of how agent shopping could reshape booking experiences.

items.title: Humans plus AI often add no synergy
summary: Combining AI and humans produces no synergy, and AI alone is often best.
AI meets 99 percent of design brief criteria but sticks to a house style.
Toggle groups beat dropdowns for small sets of options.

why.ai-interaction: It challenges the assumption that a human in the loop always improves results.
why.craft: The toggle group tip is a quick, usable interface guideline.
why.general: A mixed roundup with one practical UI rule.

items.title: Claude Code and Obsidian as a family AI brain
summary: Scott Farrar stores context in Markdown files he can inspect and correct.
He argues chat suffers from memory drift, not a lack of intelligence.
Raw unstructured input works when the system organizes the files.

why.ai-interaction: Persistent, inspectable memory is a useful pattern for designing agent experiences.
why.general: A hands-on example of keeping AI context transparent.

items.title: Lyssna adds custom branding for shared studies
summary: Add your logo, colors, welcome image and screen copy to studies.
Applies to studies shared with participants you recruit yourself.
Set defaults once and run multiple brands on Enterprise.

why.research: Branded studies help your own customers recognize and trust the study from the first screen.
why.general: A small tool update for teams running research with their own network.

items.title: If AI works from anywhere, why commute to watch it
summary: The author questions what return to office is winning people back to do.
Research showed conversation drops sharply beyond about fifty feet of distance.
Making now happens with AI, so the old case for the office weakens.

why.leadership: It gives leads a sharper way to think about the purpose of in-person time.
why.industry: Return to office debates are shifting as AI changes where work gets made.
why.general: An opinion piece on how work location arguments are changing.

items.title: What Giorgia Lupi learned on the yoga mat and at the painting table
summary: The designer describes yoga as a practice where each pose prepares the next.
In her painting studio she works without knowing what comes next.
Tolerating not knowing now shapes how she approaches her creative work.

why.craft: A personal look at how creative practice outside design feeds design work.
why.leadership: Offers a reflective view on comfort with uncertainty.
why.general: A slower read about creative habits.
